summary: CrewPulse is a daily health check-in for astronauts on missions where Earth is minutes away. Each morning, a crew member enters smart-ring data, a blood-pressure reading, four short questions, a symptom body map and a reaction test. CrewPulse compares every value with that person’s own pre-flight baseline. When something drifts, it explains in plain language why, on which data, what to do now, when to check again and who to call, citing the NASA source. One app serves three roles: the astronaut, the onboard Crew Medical Officer and the flight surgeon on Earth. Each role sees only what it should, and messages to Earth arrive with the real light-time delay from NASA/JPL Horizons.
details:
What it does

On Mars, a question to the flight surgeon and its answer take at least 22 minutes, so the crew must notice problems and act first. CrewPulse supports them with a short morning check-in: about 7 minutes with the full 3-minute reaction test, under 4 with the quick one. It answers four questions in plain language:

- How am I today?

- Why is this flagged, and on which data?

- What can I do now?

- When should I check again, and when should I call the medical officer or the ground?

How it works

Personal baseline --> Fourteen pre-flight days define each crew member’s normal: a mean and a standard deviation with a floor. Values are judged against that person, not against a population threshold.

Explainable rules --> Six rules, each tied to a NASA risk or standard:

- sleep debt, using the validated PVT-B reaction test;

- headache combined with cabin CO₂;

- cabin CO₂ advisory;

- solar particle event;

- stress and mood;

- baseline drift.

A deviation must last two days before it is flagged, which keeps false alarms down. Every alert says why, what to do, when to recheck and when to escalate, and cites its source.

Privacy by role -->

- The astronaut sees their own data.

- The Crew Medical Officer is a crewmate. They see the physical picture, but not stress and mood unless the astronaut chooses to share them.

- The flight surgeon sees everything, with the communication delay.

If a private wellbeing alert becomes urgent, the medical officer receives only “contact this crew member today”, with no details.

Real distance --> Messages between the vehicle and Earth travel with the light-time for the chosen date and destination (ISS, Moon or Mars), computed from NASA/JPL Horizons. Radiation dose and limits change with the destination.

Interactive check-in --> The check-in has six parts:

- smart-ring sync (simulated);

- blood pressure;

- sleep, fatigue, stress and mood scales;

- a front-and-back body map for symptoms, with male and female figures;

- medication;

- a reaction test: the validated 3-minute PVT-B, or a 30-second quick check that never triggers an alert on its own.

Demo scenario --> Fourteen simulated days on Mars, 1–14 November 2026, with four crew members:

- A01 builds up sleep debt and gets a headache while cabin CO₂ is above the NASA limit, the day before an EVA.

- On day 12 the whole crew lives through a replay of the real 20 May 2024 solar storm, as Curiosity measured it on Mars. The advice is to shelter now and postpone the EVA.

- A02’s stress rises in private. On day 13 the medical officer is told only to contact A02 that day.

- A04 stays within baseline throughout. A04 is the control: it shows that the rules stay quiet when nothing is wrong.

Judges can switch role, day and destination, and do a full check-in themselves.

Benefits -->

- Autonomy. The advice is written for the crew, who must act before Earth can answer.

- Fewer false alarms. Personal baselines and the two-day persistence rule filter out normal day-to-day variation.

- Honest reporting. Stress and mood stay private by default, so a crew member can report them without a crewmate reading them.

- Trust. There is no black box: every number links to its source. The app never diagnoses and never decides fitness for duty.

What we hope to achieve --> Next, we would like to:

- connect real wearables;

- enforce the role policy on a server, with encryption for each role;

- review the rules with flight surgeons;

- test the check-in during analogue missions.

Tools -->

- App: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts and lucide-react.

- Data: Python (standard library only) simulates the scenario and fetches the NASA data.

- Tests: Vitest runs 33 automated tests of the alert engine.

- Deployment: GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages.

There is no backend. The app is static and works offline once loaded, which suits a system meant to work far from Earth.

Source code, documentation and full references: https://github.com/claudiotrischitta-web/CrewPulse

Use of AI --> We used Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, under our direction. It helped us research the NASA sources, draft the architecture and the code, tests and documentation. The team chose the concept, the three-role privacy model and the scenario, reviewed and tested every part, and is responsible for it. No image, audio or video generators were used: the demo video is a screen recording of the app. Every commit in the repository is marked “Co-Authored-By: Claude”
